prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- The commander of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia's Force 47 told reporters in Bogota Monday -- a day after surrendering -- that "the solution is not through war. There must be dialogue." Nelly Avila Moreno, center, alias Karina, is escorted by soldiers after surrendering. Nelly Avila Moreno, 45, whose nom de guerre was Karina, said she and her longtime male companion made the decision jointly to abandon the FARC group, based in the jungle, at 5 a.m. Sunday. She said pressure from Colombian soldiers had been key to their decision, and she called on her fellow rebels to follow her example. "I invite them to change the sensibility that is among the guerrillas," she said, seated by her companion, who said nothing during the news conference. She also had a message for the Colombian people: "It is important to do something for peace in Colombia, and that need to do something is precisely one of my motivations." After 24 years with the FARC, Karina said she wants to reintegrate with society. "At this moment, what I am thinking about is reuniting with my family and with all of society," she said. Karina said she had had no contact with the group's leaders for the past two years. During that time, she said, "I was trying to stay alive." She said she knows nothing about the group's leaders, because "everything in the FARC is very compartmentalized." Still, she did hear through the news media about the killing by another member of FARC of Ivan Rios, a member of the group's central high command. "We suffered a very strong blow," she said. She acknowledged that news led her to worry about the possibility that one of her fellow guerrillas might consider doing the same thing to her. "A person has a lot of combatants alongside, but you don't know what each one is thinking," she said. Asked about news reports of guerrilla operations she may have participated in, Karina admitted to nothing. "They accuse me of a lot of things I wasn't part of," she said. But Miguel Antonio Paez told CNN en Espanol that he remembers well the woman who, with a band of guerrillas, stopped the bus he was on in 2004 in northwest Colombia, ordered him and the other passengers off and the bus be burned. "The commander of that guerrilla group -- a dark-haired woman, tall, with one eye missing -- called herself Karina," he said. "She ordered me tied up. Here, I have the marks from the wires, and there, while I was tied up, she lopped off my penis and testicles and I remained castrated for all my life." Asked specifically about the killing of the father of President Alvaro Uribe in 1983, she said she did not know who carried out the act, and added, "I don't have my hands stained in that deed." She said that with her surrender have come new fears about possible retribution from FARC loyalists, who consider her a traitor. Wearing a red sweatshirt and what appeared to be a diamond earring in her left ear, she said she once believed the FARC would rule Colombia. "I once dreamed of that," she said. Gen. Mario Montoya, chief of the army, said two Colombian air force helicopters were sent Sunday to pick up Karina and her companion, who had given authorities their general location. "With this, we have given a confounding strike to the FARC structure," particularly to Front 47, which at this point is practically dismantled," he said. Since the killing of Rios, 45 members of the group have laid down their arms and accepted a government plan for reinstallation into society, he said. "We want to send a message to all members of FARC who persist in the mountains," he said. "To tell them, what Karina has done is the road all the members of FARC should go down. If they don't, we are going to continue combating them. Today, more than ever, I invite them to lay down their arms, take the plan. We don't want them dead. We want them alive."

**BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) --** The commander of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia’s 47th Front told reporters in Bogota on Monday—one day after surrendering—that “the solution is not through war. There must be dialogue.”

*Nelly Avila Moreno, center, also known as Karina, is escorted by soldiers after surrendering.*

Nelly Avila Moreno, 45, whose nom de guerre was Karina, said she and her longtime male companion jointly decided at 5 a.m. Sunday to abandon the jungle-based FARC. She said pressure from Colombian soldiers had been a key factor in their decision and called on her fellow rebels to follow her example.

“I invite them to change the sensibility that is among the guerrillas,” she said, seated beside her companion, who remained silent throughout the news conference.

She also had a message for the Colombian people: “It is important to do something for peace in Colombia, and that need to do something is precisely one of my motivations.”

After 24 years with the FARC, Karina said she wants to reintegrate into society.

“At this moment, what I am thinking about is reuniting with my family and with all of society,” she said.

Karina said she had had no contact with the group’s leaders for the past two years. During that time, she said, “I was trying to stay alive.”

She said she knew nothing about the group’s leaders because “everything in the FARC is very compartmentalized.”

Still, she learned through news reports that Ivan Rios, a member of the group’s central high command, had been killed by another FARC member.

“We suffered a very strong blow,” she said.

She acknowledged that the news led her to worry that one of her fellow guerrillas might consider doing the same to her.

“A person has a lot of combatants alongside, but you don’t know what each one is thinking,” she said.

Asked about news reports concerning guerrilla operations in which she may have participated, Karina admitted to nothing.

“They accuse me of a lot of things I wasn’t part of,” she said.

But Miguel Antonio Paez told CNN en Espanol that he vividly remembered the woman who, accompanied by a band of guerrillas, stopped the bus he was traveling on in northwestern Colombia in 2004, ordered him and the other passengers off, and directed that the bus be burned.

“The commander of that guerrilla group—a dark-haired woman, tall, with one eye missing—called herself Karina,” he said. “She ordered me tied up. Here, I have the marks from the wires, and there, while I was tied up, she lopped off my penis and testicles, and I remained castrated for all my life.”

Asked specifically about the 1983 killing of President Alvaro Uribe’s father, she said she did not know who had carried out the act, adding, “I don’t have my hands stained in that deed.”

She said her surrender had brought new fears of possible retribution from FARC loyalists, who consider her a traitor.

Wearing a red sweatshirt and what appeared to be a diamond earring in her left ear, she said she had once believed the FARC would rule Colombia.

“I once dreamed of that,” she said.

Gen. Mario Montoya, chief of the army, said two Colombian air force helicopters were dispatched Sunday to pick up Karina and her companion after they provided authorities with their general location.

“With this, we have dealt a resounding blow to the FARC structure, particularly to Front 47, which at this point is practically dismantled,” he said.

Since Rios was killed, 45 members of the group have laid down their arms and accepted a government plan for reintegration into society, Montoya said.

“We want to send a message to all members of FARC who persist in the mountains,” he said. “To tell them, what Karina has done is the road all the members of FARC should go down. If they don’t, we are going to continue combating them. Today, more than ever, I invite them to lay down their arms, take the plan. We don’t want them dead. We want them alive.”

BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) — One day after giving herself up, the leader of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia’s Front 47 told journalists in Bogota on Monday that Colombia’s conflict could not be resolved by fighting and instead required negotiations.

“The answer does not lie in war. There has to be dialogue,” said Nelly Avila Moreno, 45, better known by her guerrilla alias, Karina.

Avila Moreno, who was escorted by soldiers following her surrender, said she and her longtime male partner jointly decided to leave the jungle-based FARC at 5 a.m. Sunday. According to her, military pressure from Colombian forces played a major role in that choice.

Sitting beside her silent companion at the news conference, she urged other rebels to do the same and called on them to alter the mindset prevailing within the guerrilla movement.

She also addressed Colombians directly, saying that contributing to peace in the country was important and that the need to act had been among the reasons behind her surrender.

After spending 24 years in the FARC, Karina said she now hoped to return to civilian life. Her immediate thoughts, she said, were focused on reuniting with her family and reintegrating into society as a whole.

Karina said she had not communicated with the organization’s senior leadership for two years. During that period, she said, her main concern had been staying alive. She added that she had little information about FARC commanders because the organization operated through tightly separated compartments.

She nevertheless learned from news reports that Ivan Rios, a member of the FARC’s central high command, had been killed by another rebel. She described his death as an extremely severe setback for the group.

Karina acknowledged that the incident made her fear that one of the fighters around her might contemplate taking similar action against her. A commander could be surrounded by many combatants, she said, without knowing what any individual among them was thinking.

When questioned about reported guerrilla actions in which she allegedly took part, Karina accepted no responsibility, saying she had been blamed for numerous incidents with which she had no involvement.

Miguel Antonio Paez, however, told CNN en Español that he clearly remembered a woman he identified as Karina. Paez said that in 2004, in northwestern Colombia, a guerrilla unit stopped the bus on which he was traveling, forced him and the other passengers to get off, and ordered the vehicle burned.

He described the unit’s commander as a tall, dark-haired woman missing one eye who called herself Karina. Paez alleged that she ordered guerrillas to bind him with wire and, while he was restrained, cut off his penis and testicles, leaving him permanently castrated. He said marks from the wire remained visible.

Asked directly about the 1983 killing of President Alvaro Uribe’s father, Karina said she did not know who committed it and denied having blood on her hands in connection with the act.

She said surrendering had brought a different set of fears, including the possibility of retaliation by FARC loyalists who viewed her as a traitor.

Dressed in a red sweatshirt and wearing what appeared to be a diamond earring in her left ear, Karina said she had once believed the FARC would eventually govern Colombia. She acknowledged that this had once been her dream.

Army commander Gen. Mario Montoya said two Colombian air force helicopters were dispatched Sunday to retrieve Karina and her companion after they provided authorities with a general description of where they were located.

Montoya called the surrender a decisive blow against the FARC’s structure, especially Front 47, which he said was now nearly dismantled.

He added that since Rios was killed, 45 members of the organization had surrendered their weapons and entered a government program designed to help them return to society.

Montoya also directed a warning and an appeal to FARC members who remained in the mountains. He said Karina’s decision represented the route every rebel should take; those who refused would continue to face military action. Urging them more strongly than ever to disarm and join the government program, he said authorities did not want them killed but wanted them to survive.

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia** — Nelly Ávila Moreno, better known by her nom de guerre “Karina,” surrendered to Colombian authorities Monday, marking a significant blow to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC.

Ávila Moreno, commander of the guerrilla group’s 47th Front, turned herself in in the northwestern department of Antioquia after years of fighting government forces. Colombian officials described her as one of the FARC’s most prominent female commanders.

Following her surrender, Ávila Moreno called for dialogue and a peaceful resolution to Colombia’s decades-long conflict. She also urged other guerrillas to consider leaving the armed struggle, according to statements released by authorities.

The former commander had been accused of involvement in kidnappings, killings and attacks on security forces. She was reportedly under intense military pressure before surrendering, as government operations and internal desertions weakened FARC units in the region.

Colombian officials portrayed the move as evidence that the insurgency’s command structure was deteriorating. At the time, the FARC was facing a series of setbacks, including the deaths of senior leaders and growing pressure to release hostages.

The FARC began as a Marxist peasant movement in the 1960s and became Latin America’s largest rebel organization. Colombia’s conflict killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions before the government and the group signed a peace agreement in 2016.

Karina denied some of the most sensational accusations made against her, including claims that she had participated in the 1983 killing of President Álvaro Uribe’s father. Authorities nevertheless alleged that forces under her command had committed murders, kidnappings, extortion, attacks on towns and security units, and other abuses. She had acquired a reputation in official accounts as an especially ruthless commander, although she disputed that portrayal.

The Colombian army presented the surrender as evidence that its campaign was weakening and fragmenting the FARC. Army commander **Gen. Mario Montoya** described it as a major blow to the guerrillas and appealed to remaining fighters to demobilize. Army commander General Mario Montoya used the surrender to renew the government’s appeal to other insurgents.

“Demobilize,” Montoya said, promising that rebels who laid down their weapons would be treated humanely and could benefit from government reintegration programs. He said the security forces would guarantee the lives of those who surrendered.

Ávila Moreno had spent decades in the FARC and was accused by Colombian authorities of involvement in killings, kidnappings and attacks in Antioquia and neighboring areas. counterfactuals.output:
## Military pressure, Ríos killing helped drive FARC commander Karina to surrender

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia —** Sustained military operations, mounting desertions and the killing of senior Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia commander Iván Ríos combined to push veteran guerrilla leader Elda Neyis Mosquera, known as **“Karina,”** into surrendering and left the FARC’s 47th Front close to collapse.

Karina, one of the insurgency’s best-known female commanders, surrendered to Colombian authorities in May 2008 in Antioquia after roughly two decades in the FARC. She had led the 47th Front, which operated mainly in parts of Antioquia and Caldas and had been blamed for killings, kidnappings, forced recruitment and attacks on security forces and civilians.

### Relentless operations weakened the front

In the period before her surrender, Colombian troops intensified operations against Karina’s units, limiting their movement and disrupting their access to food, medicine, communications and reinforcements. Soldiers tracked smaller guerrilla groups through difficult rural terrain while the government offered rewards and reintegration benefits to fighters who deserted.

The pressure produced a steady loss of personnel. Some combatants were killed or captured, while others abandoned the organization and provided intelligence about camps, routes and commanders. Each defection further reduced the front’s ability to maintain security and increased Karina’s fear that the military was closing in.

By the time she surrendered, the 47th Front had reportedly been reduced from a substantial regional force to a small, fragmented group. Its command structure, logistical networks and capacity to mount coordinated attacks had been badly damaged. Colombian officials described the unit as nearly dismantled.

### Ríos’ death underscored internal breakdown

The March 2008 killing of **Iván Ríos**, a member of the FARC’s seven-person ruling Secretariat, added a powerful psychological blow. Ríos, whose real name was Manuel Jesús Muñoz Ortiz, was killed by one of his own security guards, who later turned himself in and presented evidence of the commander’s death.

Ríos had exercised authority over FARC forces in the region and was associated with the command structure above Karina. His death showed that even senior leaders were vulnerable—not only to military pursuit but also to betrayal by their own fighters.

For Karina, the episode reinforced the danger of remaining in the field. It demonstrated that government pressure and reward programs were eroding loyalty inside guerrilla units. Fighters responsible for protecting commanders could instead kill them and defect, making traditional FARC security arrangements increasingly unreliable.

The killing also deprived regional units of senior leadership and coordination at a time when military operations were already isolating them. Combined with the deaths and capture of other guerrillas, it weakened morale and contributed to a sense that the FARC’s command network was unraveling.

### Isolation and fear of betrayal

Officials said Karina ultimately faced several converging threats: capture or death in combat, betrayal by subordinates, and possible punishment from within the FARC for the losses suffered by her front. Cut off from reliable support and commanding a sharply diminished force, she chose to seek government protection.

She surrendered with another guerrilla after contacts were established with authorities. The government portrayed the event as evidence that its combination of military pressure, intelligence operations, rewards and demobilization programs was working.

Karina’s surrender did not by itself end all FARC activity in the region, but it removed the 47th Front’s most recognizable commander and accelerated the unit’s disintegration. The sequence—from sustained army pressure and repeated desertions to Ríos’ killing and Karina’s capitulation—illustrated how battlefield losses and internal mistrust were reinforcing each other inside the insurgency.

Her surrender came during one of the FARC’s most damaging periods. Within a few months, the organization had lost Ríos, Secretariat member Raúl Reyes and founder Manuel Marulanda, while security forces continued to penetrate guerrilla communications and territorial strongholds. Against that backdrop, Karina’s decision became both a practical consequence of the 47th Front’s collapse and a symbol of the broader crisis facing the FARC leadership.
